// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["AE75F0D82BA3DF824FBFC69340CC3B4D66C598373B1AB54CDB6C8BFD83A6B961", "7B2A3F5C96F95BD8086CE54B0825E300F9C8F11FE3401BB631B3215C8DE9EB10", "EB86FA1386FE6E4533B8B938DCC1250616D2F1C14C15E2FCF80834A161018A0A", "FD23D6E57DE6F4E1F9D7118DA1C5F31A8AF6BE5E5D9E8170F9493447268D50C5", "A0DE9333442C1BF9349A460141AE5E80F911955C6506040FA3D021BF6C1AE3E4", "95B6D71FC0C0F8C5E1533A37AEF92CF6B0C961E2CC612A97117FA6759CE5FC06", "236A9CB0D71951C36398A32EB660CE2CD4A52CCFA7CF751CC6A35D9DE549E19B", "5E594C448760A3135B1A3A83E07A4F2E6FBE49414EF2C7CAB1CBA77F284FA63B", "8A964D5F8373948D20A1D4296FB92E545DAD4617A0C810F3B934B53D98AE8963", "410260B1B6F5AF5FBEEB9EA3220658435E876CB3247126EE907A437F312DB373", "96275DFD6282A522B011177EE049296952AC794832091F937FBBF92869028629"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kimai authenticated session activity with no preceding form-login POST (forged remember-me cookie) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Kimai (Symfony) authenticated access to admin/API/user routes from a source IP that never submitted a POST to the login form in the lookback window. CVE-2026-52824 lets an attacker with the publicly-known default APP_SECRET forge the KIMAI_REMEMBER cookie and be silently auto-authenticated, so the account 'logs in' without any credential submission crossing the wire. Rationale: Uses Kimai's KIMAI_REMEMBER remember-me cookie name and Symfony's form-login POST as the two anchors from the article; the anti-join (authenticated route access from an IP that never POSTed to login) is the observable footprint of a forged remember-me cookie since Symfony auto-authenticates without a credential exchange. Cross-checked GitLab advisory and Symfony login docs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/kimai/kimai/CVE-2026-52824/ • https://symfony.com/doc/current/security/login_link.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1550.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 'remember me' users whose original POST /login happened before the lookback window began
  • SSO / reverse-proxy that terminates auth upstream and forwards without a Kimai form POST
  • Corporate NAT egress where one IP both logs in and is reused by an automation account
  • Health-check / monitoring probes hitting /api with a stored service session
  • Load balancer or CDN rewriting the client source IP so the login POST and the app request appear on different IPs
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "HealthCheck" and UserAgent !has "kube-probe" and CIp !in (dynamic(["<corporate-egress-not-needed:leave-empty-or-populate-org-CIDRs-in-loginIPs-let>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the CIp's full request timeline; confirm the first authenticated request truly has no prior POST to /login and inspect whether Cookie carried KIMAI_REMEMBER but never a fresh PHPSESSID handshake. Identify which Kimai account (CsUsername) the session maps to and whether it is super_admin. 2) Contain: rotate APP_SECRET immediately (invalidates all forged cookies/links), force-logout all sessions, and require password reset + enable 2FA on privileged accounts. 3) Hunt: check whether the same IP/UA hit login-link URLs (hash/expires/user params) or created users, changed rates, or exported timesheets; confirm the instance was on Kimai < 2.58.0 with the default secret.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let loginIPs = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where CsMethod == "POST" and CsUriStem has "login"   // Kimai/Symfony form-login check route
    | distinct CIp;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where CsUriStem has_any ("/admin/", "/api/", "/user")   // authenticated Kimai surfaces
| where ScStatus >= 200 and ScStatus < 400
| where CsUsername != "" or Cookie has "KIMAI_REMEMBER"    // session was authenticated
| where CIp !in (loginIPs)                                 // but no form login ever seen from this IP
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(CsUriStem, 20) by CIp, UserAgent, CsUsername
| order by FirstSeen desc

Kimai forged Symfony login-link request (user+expires+hash signed URL) to super_admin AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound GET requests whose query string carries the Symfony passwordless login-link signature triad — user, expires and hash. With the default APP_SECRET (CVE-2026-52824) an unauthenticated attacker can mint valid login links for any account, so a burst of these signed URLs (especially targeting the id=1/super_admin identifier) from external IPs is a direct forgery indicator. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit 'LoginLink signatures' forgery vector and the Symfony-documented login-link parameter triad (user/expires/hash); matching all three tokens in the query string is a distinctive single-event signature that fires even without knowing Kimai's exact check-route path. Cross-checked Symfony login-link docs and the GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/kimai/kimai/CVE-2026-52824/ • https://symfony.com/doc/current/security/login_link.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organisation legitimately uses Symfony/Kimai passwordless login links for real users
  • Password-reset or email-verification links that reuse a similar signed-URL shape
  • Security scanners (Burp/ZAP) fuzzing query parameters named user/expires/hash
  • Uptime monitors replaying a captured login-link URL
  • Other Symfony apps behind the same proxy emitting UriSigner-style links
Suppression filter
| where CsUriStem !has "password-reset" and UserAgent !has_any ("ZAP", "Burp", "Nuclei", "masscan")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract TargetUser from CsUriQuery; determine whether the value corresponds to the id=1/super_admin username and whether the request returned 200/302 (link accepted). Check the source IP's geo/ASN and whether it is external. 2) Contain: if the login link was accepted, rotate APP_SECRET (invalidates every forged link), kill active sessions, reset the targeted account's password and enforce 2FA. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same CIp/UA for subsequent authenticated admin/API activity and for KIMAI_REMEMBER-cookie sessions; verify the deployment ran the default APP_SECRET on Kimai < 2.58.0.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where CsMethod == "GET"
| where CsUriQuery has "hash=" and CsUriQuery has "expires=" and CsUriQuery has "user="   // Symfony login-link signed URL triad
| extend TargetUser = extract(@"(?i)user=([^&]+)", 1, CsUriQuery)
| project TimeGenerated, CIp, UserAgent, CsUriStem, CsUriQuery, TargetUser, ScStatus, CsUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FacturaScripts CVE-2026-47677: high-volume brute-force of /login two-factor-validation endpoint AIExploitation High
Hunts an unauthenticated attacker hammering the FacturaScripts `/login` endpoint with `action=two-factor-validation` POSTs to guess one of the ~17 simultaneously-valid TOTP codes. A legitimate user submits 1-3 codes; the published PoC sustains ~400 requests/sec from a single source IP, so a per-IP request count on this exact endpoint is a clean, article-specific signal. Rationale: Anchors on the exact vulnerable endpoint path `/login` plus the `two-factor-validation` action string and POST method from the advisory; per-source-IP volume >20 in 5m is far above any human 2FA flow but far below the PoC's sustained rate. Cross-checked against the GitLab Advisory Database entry which confirms the endpoint and unauthenticated-POST shape. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/facturascripts/facturascripts/CVE-2026-47677/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c67f-gmxw-mj93
ATT&CKT1110 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated uptime/synthetic monitor probing /login on a loop
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) or authorized pentest replaying the CVE PoC
  • Load-testing tool (JMeter/k6) run against the FacturaScripts login path
  • Shared-NAT egress (many corporate users behind one public IP) inflating per-IP counts
  • Broken SSO/mobile client retrying 2FA submission in a tight loop
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<scanner_ip_allowlist>")   // OPTIONAL: replace with your authorized scanner/monitoring egress IPs; omit this line if you have none
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the SourceIP is external and the RequestURL targets `/login` + `two-factor-validation`; pull the full request timeline and count 302 responses (a 302 = fsLogkey session issued = takeover). Identify which `fsNick` values were targeted (body/query param). 2) CONTAIN: Block the SourceIP at the WAF/reverse proxy, force-expire sessions (rotate fsLogkey / clear session store), and upgrade FacturaScripts to 2026.3.0 which patches the endpoint. 3) HUNT: For any nick that received a 302, review that account's post-login activity (invoice/customer/API-key access, config changes) and check for the same brute pattern from other IPs / against other nicks.
CommonSecurityLog

| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/login"
| where RequestURL has "two-factor-validation"
| summarize Attempts = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), TargetHosts = dcount(DestinationHostName) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Attempts > 20   // legit 2FA submits 1-3 codes; CVE-2026-47677 PoC sustains ~400 rps from one IP
| order by Attempts desc
source:linux.syslog "/login" "two-factor-validation"

FacturaScripts 'two-factor-code-invalid' application-log flood (distributed 2FA brute-force / account-lockout DoS) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact warning literal `two-factor-code-invalid` that `twoFactorValidationAction()` writes to the FacturaScripts log on every failed TOTP guess. Counting these per host catches the brute-force even when the attacker rotates source IPs (invisible to a per-IP web-log rule) and also surfaces the availability side-effect: 6 failures (MAX_INCIDENT_COUNT) lock the legitimate user out of loginAction for 10 minutes. Rationale: Uses the verbatim `Tools::log()->warning('two-factor-code-invalid')` string from the vulnerable code path, so it is essentially FP-free except for genuine failed 2FA attempts; the >20/5m threshold distinguishes a brute-force flood from occasional user typos. Confirmed against the GitLab advisory's reproduction of the handler. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/facturascripts/facturascripts/CVE-2026-47677/
ATT&CKT1110 T1531
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A single legitimate user repeatedly fat-fingering their TOTP code (a handful, not dozens)
  • Clock drift between the TOTP app and server causing genuine repeated failures for one nick
  • QA/staging test suite exercising the 2FA flow with bad codes
  • Authorized pentest replaying the PoC
  • Log duplication (same event shipped by two collectors) inflating counts
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the targeted `fsNick`(s) and whether failures cluster on admin/company nicks (public info per the advisory); check the host's web logs for the corresponding /login two-factor-validation POST burst and any 302. 2) CONTAIN: Patch to FacturaScripts 2026.3.0, block offending IP(s) at the edge, and notify locked-out users (10-min loginAction lockout is expected collateral). 3) HUNT: Search for a subsequent successful login (302 / new session) for the targeted nick, and pivot on the same warning across all FacturaScripts hosts to scope multi-target campaigns.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where SyslogMessage has "two-factor-code-invalid"
| summarize FailedCodes = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Sample = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, HostIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where FailedCodes > 20   // 6 failures (MAX_INCIDENT_COUNT) already lock a nick out; sustained flood = brute-force / targeted lockout DoS
| order by FailedCodes desc
source:linux.syslog "two-factor-code-invalid"
APPLICATION
`comment("FacturaScripts PHP app warning — no CIM datamodel covers app-tier log strings; raw search")`
index=* "two-factor-code-invalid"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as failed_codes, dc(host) as hosts, latest(_raw) as sample by _time host
| where failed_codes > 20
| sort - failed_codes
FacturaScripts CVE-2026-47677: successful 2FA bypass — 302 session issuance following a brute-force burst AIActions on Objectives Medium
Confirms an actual account takeover (not just an attempt): a source IP that sent many POSTs to `/login` `two-factor-validation` AND received at least one HTTP 302 — the redirect that issues the `fsNick`+`fsLogkey` session cookie pair. The per-IP burst-count qualifier separates attacker success from the identical 302 a legitimate user gets on a normal 2FA login. Rationale: Combines the exact endpoint (`/login` + `two-factor-validation` in csUriQuery, POST) with scStatus 302 — the only status the handler returns on a valid guess (updateUserAndRedirect) — gated by a brute-force attempt count so a lone legitimate 2FA 302 doesn't fire. This is the takeover-confirmed pivot, distinct from the attempt-volume UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/facturascripts/facturascripts/CVE-2026-47677/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c67f-gmxw-mj93
ATT&CKT1078 T1110
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentest whose PoC actually lands a valid code (true positive by design, but expected during engagements)
  • Load test that both floods /login and completes a legit 2FA, producing a 302 within the same IP/window
  • Reverse proxy collapsing many internal users to one cIP so a legit 302 co-occurs with high attempt counts (tune with X-Forwarded-For)
  • Scanner that follows redirects and happens to trip a valid code during a long run
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("<scanner_ip_allowlist>")   // OPTIONAL: exclude authorized scanner/pentest egress IPs; omit if none
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Treat as confirmed takeover — capture cIP, sSiteName, targeted `fsNick`, and the 302 timestamp; correlate with the `two-factor-code-invalid` flood (companion UC) to confirm the preceding brute-force. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately invalidate the issued session (rotate/clear fsLogkey server-side), disable/reset the affected account, block cIP, and patch to 2026.3.0. 3) HUNT: Enumerate everything the hijacked identity touched after the 302 — invoice/customer/supplier reads, record edits/deletes, API-key and plugin-config access — and check whether other nicks received a 302 from the same or related IPs.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem =~ "/login"
| where csUriQuery has "two-factor-validation"
| summarize Attempts = count(), Successes = countif(scStatus == 302), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleAgent = any(csUserAgent) by cIP, sSiteName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where Attempts > 20 and Successes > 0   // 302 = fsLogkey issued; >20 attempts in 10m rules out a normal human 2FA login. If Apache/Nginx: point at AppServiceHTTPLogs (ScStatus/CIp) or your reverse-proxy access-log table.
| order by LastSeen desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Shai-Hulud npm worm payload/workflow file drop (bundle.js, setup_bun.js, shai-hulud-workflow.yml) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Shai-Hulud credential exfiltration: node/npm outbound to webhook.site
Shai-Hulud npm worm payload/workflow file drop (bundle.js, setup_bun.js, shai-hulud-workflow.yml) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Shai-Hulud supply-chain worm dropping its self-replicating payload and CI persistence file onto developer machines during npm install. Fires on the confirmed malicious bundle.js SHA256 or the distinctive worm filenames written by node/npm. Rationale: Uses the second-source-confirmed Shai-Hulud bundle.js SHA256 (46faab8a...) and the campaign's distinctive filenames (shai-hulud-workflow.yml, setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js) named across Unit42/Wiz/Datadog write-ups of the article's flagship campaign; hash+filename anchors make this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately named a file bundle.js under a non-malicious .github/workflows path (rare — that dir holds YAML, not JS)
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating a Shai-Hulud sample in a sandbox/analysis VM
  • EDR/AV quarantine copies of the payload re-triggering the file-write event from the quarantine folder
  • Threat-intel/IR team staging IOC files named setup_bun.js for tabletop or purple-team exercises
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Windows Defender\", @"\Quarantine\") or DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName node.exe/npm) and the folder — a real hit is bundle.js/setup_bun.js executed during an npm/bun install in a repo working dir. Check the file SHA256 against 46faab8a... 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, revoke and rotate all npm tokens, GitHub PATs, and cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure) keys used from it; check GitHub for a newly-created public repo named 'Shai-Hulud' and any 'shai-hulud-workflow.yml' pushed to your repos. 3) HUNT: Pivot to outbound connections to webhook.site from the same host, enumerate every package version installed in the last 24h, and scope other developers who installed the same dependency.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (SHA256 == "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09")
     or FileName in~ ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
     or (FileName =~ "bundle.js" and FolderPath has @"\.github\workflows")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileSHA256 == "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09")
     or TargetFileName in~ ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
     or (TargetFileName =~ "bundle.js" and TargetFilePath has @"\.github\workflows")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Shai-Hulud npm Worm Payload and Workflow File Written
id: 6f2c1e94-8a13-4b77-9d2e-7c5a1f0b3d21
description: Detects the Shai-Hulud self-replicating npm worm dropping its payload (bundle.js) or CI persistence/2.0 payload files on disk
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/aikido-intel-detects-malware-vulnerabilities-first
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
  - https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_hash:
    Hashes|contains: '46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09'
  selection_names:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\shai-hulud-workflow.yml'
      - '\setup_bun.js'
      - '\bun_environment.js'
  condition: selection_hash or selection_names
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\shai-hulud-workflow.yml OR *\setup_bun.js OR *\bun_environment.js OR *\Setup_Bun.js) OR @Hashes:*46FAAB8AB153FAE6E80E7CCA38EAB363075BB524EDD79E42269217A083628F09*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(shai-hulud-workflow\.yml|setup_bun\.js|bun_environment\.js)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js") OR Filesystem.file_hash="46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09" OR (Filesystem.file_name="bundle.js" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\.github\\workflows\\*")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js") OR Filesystem.file_hash="46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09" OR (Filesystem.file_name="bundle.js" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\.github\\workflows\\*")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Shai-Hulud credential exfiltration: node/npm outbound to webhook.site AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Shai-Hulud worm's credential exfiltration stage where the postinstall payload beacons harvested npm/GitHub/cloud tokens to the hardcoded webhook.site drop (bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7). Pairs the webhook.site destination with a node/npm/bun/git initiating process to cut the FP from legit webhook testing. Rationale: Anchors on the second-source-confirmed hardcoded exfil host webhook.site (Shai-Hulud endpoint bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7) but requires a node/npm/bun/git initiating process so it fires on postinstall exfil, not a developer manually testing a webhook in a browser. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1567 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using webhook.site to test an outbound webhook from a Node app during development
  • CI runner (node/git) hitting a webhook.site URL configured in a test suite or integration fixture
  • QA automation posting to webhook.site as a capture endpoint
  • Internal tooling that uses webhook.site free-tier bins for prototyping event delivery
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","postinstall","ci","exec") and not (DeviceName has_any ("build-agent","ci-runner") and InitiatingProcessAccountName has "jenkins")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full RemoteUrl/DNS path — a real hit posts to a webhook.site UUID bin (campaign default bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7) shortly after an npm/bun install; check InitiatingProcessCommandLine for a package install and correlate with a bundle.js/setup_bun.js write in the last hour. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, immediately rotate npm tokens, GitHub PATs, and AWS/GCP/Azure keys from that machine, and block webhook.site at egress. 3) HUNT: Search GitHub audit for a new public 'Shai-Hulud' repo or 'shai-hulud-workflow.yml' commits under affected users, and scope every other host that installed the same package version.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "webhook.site"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","bun.exe","git.exe","curl.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "webhook.site"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or SHA1 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or MD5 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or SHA1 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or MD5 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] DIRAC FileCatalog checkDataset SQL injection carrying Python eval gadget (CVE-2026-61667)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] DIRAC FileCatalog service Python process spawns shell or recon binary (eval RCE)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Post-RCE read of DIRAC dirac.cfg / proxy / token stores on FileCatalog host · [LLM] DIRAC dirac.cfg/proxy access followed by outbound egress from service process (exfiltration) · [LLM] DIRAC service process deletes or truncates its own logs (anti-forensics post-RCE)
DIRAC FileCatalog checkDataset SQL injection carrying Python eval gadget (CVE-2026-61667) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts DIRAC FileCatalog / DatasetManager service logs for checkDataset requests whose datasets parameter contains SQL-injection tokens (UNION/SELECT/quote-break) combined with a Python eval gadget (__import__/os.system/subprocess). This is the exact CVE-2026-61667 vector where the injected SQL result is passed straight to eval() for RCE. Rationale: Uses the article's named function `checkDataset` and `DatasetManager` FileCatalog components plus the eval-gadget strings an attacker must return through the SQLi (__import__/os.system) — a combination that never appears in a benign dataset name. Defender/Falcon left empty because DIRAC application/DB logs are not shipped to Defender XDR or the Falcon FDR. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/ • https://dailycve.com/dirac-filecatalog-datasetmanager-remote-code-execution-rce-via-sql-injection-eval-cve-2026-61667-critical-dc-jul2026-956/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A pentester or vuln-scanner (e.g. sqlmap) probing the FileCatalog endpoint during an authorized assessment
  • Developer/QA testing dataset queries containing literal words like 'union' or 'select' in a legitimate dataset name
  • DIRAC integration tests that intentionally exercise malformed dataset inputs
  • A security researcher validating the CVE-2026-61667 patch on a staging node
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("sqlmap","pytest","integration-test","unittest"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request/log line and the authenticated user identity; confirm the datasets value contains both SQL syntax and a Python gadget (not just the word 'union'). Check the DIRAC version against patched 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10. 2) Contain: revoke the offending user's DIRAC proxy/token, isolate the FileCatalog host from egress, and snapshot service logs before the attacker can prune them. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for python-service→shell spawns (UC2), reads of dirac.cfg (UC3), and outbound exfil (UC4) within the same session window.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has_any ("dirac","FileCatalog","DataManagement","tornado")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("checkDataset","DatasetManager","FileCatalog")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("UNION","__import__","os.system","subprocess","commands.getoutput","eval(")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("'","\"","--","/*",";")   // quote-break / statement-stack markers
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (@process.name:*dirac* OR @process.name:*FileCatalog* OR @process.name:*tornado*) AND (checkDataset OR DatasetManager) AND (UNION OR __import__ OR os.system OR subprocess)

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`

DIRAC FileCatalog service Python process spawns shell or recon binary (eval RCE) AIInstallation High
Flagship post-exploitation detection for CVE-2026-61667: the DIRAC FileCatalog/DatasetManager service Python process (which calls eval on attacker-controlled DB output) spawning /bin/sh, bash or reconnaissance tools. Legitimately the FileCatalog service never forks a shell. Rationale: Pairs the article's named service components (FileCatalog/DatasetManager parent Python cmdline) with shell/recon children — the exact behaviour a passed-to-eval() gadget produces. Datadog/Falcon can't see the DIRAC parent cmdline (auditd EXECVE and the ProcessRollup2 reference lack parent-cmdline), so those variants scope to recon children only and are noisier — hence tier alerting rests on the Defender/Sentinel/Splunk parent-aware forms. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DIRAC administrator running maintenance scripts that legitimately shell out from a python service wrapper
  • DIRAC agents that call subprocess to invoke gfal/xrootd data-transfer CLIs during normal operation
  • Monitoring/health-check plugins that run 'uname'/'id' from the service context
  • Container entrypoint scripts where python launches bash during startup
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gfal","xrdcp","xrootd","healthcheck","/usr/libexec/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child process command line and full process tree — a benign gfal transfer looks nothing like 'sh -c id;curl'. Confirm the parent is the FileCatalog/DatasetManager service and identify the authenticated caller from correlated service logs (UC1). 2) Contain: kill the child process, isolate the host from egress, and freeze the DIRAC service user's proxies/tokens. 3) Hunt: check for dirac.cfg reads (UC3), outbound exfil (UC4) and log tampering (UC5) tied to the same PID/session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("FileCatalog","DatasetManager","dirac-service","tornado-start","DIRAC")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","cat","chmod","python","python3")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("FileCatalog","DatasetManager","dirac-service","tornado-start","DIRAC")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","cat","chmod","python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Post-RCE read of DIRAC dirac.cfg / proxy / token stores on FileCatalog host AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for a shell/python child of the DIRAC service reading or exporting dirac.cfg (which holds DB passwords) or the proxy/token stores — the article's stated objective once RCE is achieved. Scopes to file-access binaries operating on DIRAC config/credential paths. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit loot list — 'read the local dirac.cfg, get database passwords and export all stored proxies and tokens' — via the concrete dirac.cfg filename and DIRAC config/proxy paths. Medium FP because admins do legitimately read dirac.cfg; the shell/python parent constraint keeps it tight. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DIRAC sysadmin manually cat-ing dirac.cfg during troubleshooting from an interactive shell
  • Backup/config-management jobs (Ansible, rsync, tar) archiving /opt/dirac/etc
  • Legitimate dirac-proxy-init / dirac-admin tooling touching the proxy store
  • Monitoring agents parsing dirac.cfg for health metrics
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","rsync","dirac-proxy-init","dirac-admin") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("sshd","sudo"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the reader's parent is an interactive admin login or the FileCatalog service; the latter is the true positive. Cross-reference the timestamp with UC1/UC2 hits for the same host/user. 2) Contain: rotate the database credentials stored in dirac.cfg and revoke ALL proxies/tokens the service could export — assume they are compromised. 3) Hunt: look for outbound transfer of that data (UC4) and for reuse of the exported proxies/tokens against external grid resources.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac.cfg","/opt/dirac/etc","dirac-proxy","ProxyDB","proxyDB","export") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac.cfg","/opt/dirac","proxy","token")
| where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","less","more","head","tail","strings","base64","xxd","tar","scp","python","python3")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","sh","bash","dash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cat","grep","less","head","tail","strings","base64","xxd","tar","scp","python","python3")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac.cfg","/opt/dirac/etc","dirac-proxy","ProxyDB","proxyDB")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","sh","bash","dash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DIRAC dirac.cfg/proxy access followed by outbound egress from service process (exfiltration) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a read/export of dirac.cfg or the proxy/token store (UC3 vector) with an outbound public network connection from a python/shell process on the same host within 10 minutes — the exfiltration step that turns credential theft into loss. Directly maps the article's 'export all stored proxies and tokens' impact. Rationale: Two-stage correlation (credential read → outbound egress from the same host, same process class, ≤10 min) captures the article's proxy/token exfil impact without a static IOC. No Sigma/Datadog — the detection is a cross-event temporal join those single-event shapes can't express. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://dailycve.com/dirac-filecatalog-datasetmanager-remote-code-execution-rce-via-sql-injection-eval-cve-2026-61667-critical-dc-jul2026-956/
ATT&CKT1041 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DIRAC service legitimately fetching config then making outbound grid data transfers (gfal/xrootd) to public endpoints
  • Config-management pulling dirac.cfg then syncing to a remote repo/artifact store
  • Backup jobs tar-ing /opt/dirac and shipping it to off-site storage over scp/sftp
  • Monitoring agent reading config then POSTing metrics to a SaaS collector
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has_any ("xrootd","gfal","srm","eos") and RemotePort !in (1094, 2811, 8443)
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the outbound destination — a known grid SE/xrootd endpoint is likely benign; an unfamiliar cloud IP/paste site is not. Confirm the preceding config/proxy read was by the service, not an admin. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress, rotate dirac.cfg DB credentials, and revoke every proxy/token in the store. 3) Hunt: check the destination IP for reuse across other DIRAC hosts and pivot on the exported proxies being replayed against external resources.
let Window = 10m;
let CfgAccess = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac.cfg","dirac-proxy","ProxyDB","/opt/dirac/etc")
    | where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","python","python3","tar","base64","scp","curl")
    | project CfgTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, CfgCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","curl","wget","scp","sftp","bash","sh","nc","ncat")
| join kind=inner CfgAccess on DeviceName
| where Timestamp between (CfgTime .. CfgTime + Window)
| project CfgTime, NetTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, CfgCmd, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by NetTime desc
let Window = 10m;
let CfgAccess = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac.cfg","dirac-proxy","ProxyDB","/opt/dirac/etc")
    | project CfgTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, CfgCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound"
| where SrcUsername != "" or isnotempty(DstIpAddr)
| join kind=inner CfgAccess on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (CfgTime .. CfgTime + Window)
| project CfgTime, NetTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, CfgCmd, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url
| order by NetTime desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 event_platform=Lin
| ContextImageFileName=/\/(python[0-9.]*|curl|wget|scp|sftp|nc|ncat|bash|sh)$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(dirac\.cfg|dirac-proxy|ProxyDB)/i | groupBy([aid], function=count())}, field=aid, include=[aid])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK

| tstats `summariesonly` count max(_time) as netTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="outbound" All_Traffic.dest_category="public" All_Traffic.process_name IN ("python","python3","curl","wget","scp","sftp","nc","bash") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| join type=inner src [
    | tstats `summariesonly` max(_time) as cfgTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*dirac.cfg*" OR Processes.process="*dirac-proxy*" OR Processes.process="*ProxyDB*" by Processes.dest
    | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
    | rename dest as src
  ]
| where netTime > cfgTime AND (netTime - cfgTime) < 600
| eval delaySec = netTime - cfgTime
| table src dest dest_port process_name cfgTime netTime delaySec
| tstats summariesonly=false count max(_time) as netTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="outbound" All_Traffic.dest_category="public" All_Traffic.process_name IN ("python","python3","curl","wget","scp","sftp","nc","bash") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name

    | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

DIRAC service process deletes or truncates its own logs (anti-forensics post-RCE) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the DIRAC FileCatalog service (or its shell child) deleting, shredding or truncating DIRAC log files — the article's noted capability to 'remove evidence of the exploit from the log' after achieving RCE. Scopes to file-destruction binaries targeting DIRAC log paths. Rationale: Grounded in the article's stated anti-forensics capability ('remove evidence of the exploit from the log'), constrained to DIRAC log paths plus a python/shell parent so it doesn't fire on generic logrotate. Medium confidence because attacker log paths vary; the parent-process constraint is the fidelity anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/
ATT&CKT1070.002 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • logrotate or a cron cleanup job pruning old DIRAC logs (parent would be cron/logrotate, not python service)
  • A DIRAC admin manually clearing a noisy log during troubleshooting
  • CI/CD or container rebuild wiping /opt/dirac logs on redeploy
  • Disk-space remediation scripts truncating large .log files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("logrotate","cron","crond","anacron","systemd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the deleting process's parent — logrotate/cron is benign, the FileCatalog service Python or an interactive attacker shell is not. Recover deleted logs from backup/journald if possible. 2) Contain: preserve remaining forensic artifacts (auditd, EDR raw events, memory) immediately since local logs may be gone; isolate the host. 3) Hunt: reconstruct the intrusion from EDR/auditd (which the attacker cannot prune) — correlate with UC1 (SQLi), UC2 (RCE) and UC3 (credential read) to establish the full chain and blast radius.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("rm","shred","truncate","unlink","sed")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/opt/dirac","dirac","FileCatalog") and ProcessCommandLine has_any (".log","/log/","ServiceLog","serverlog")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","sh","bash","dash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("rm","shred","truncate","unlink","sed")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/opt/dirac","dirac","FileCatalog")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (".log","/log/","ServiceLog","serverlog")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","sh","bash","dash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-61667")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-61667")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
